question: The Alliance for Open Media (AOM) brings together the world’s biggest tech companies, including five that are gatekeepers under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), to develop audio/video technologies outside the recognised standards bodies, without safeguards relating to fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory (FRAND) conduct. AOM sets the price of innovation at zero: all users must contribute their patents royalty-free.

Moreover, several AOM members leverage their platforms to mandate third-party adoption of AOM technologies in consumer markets. The AOM structure undercuts existing media standards and removes the incentive to engage in independent European audio/video research and development. Ultimately, the model threatens Europe’s wider FRAND-dependent innovation base.
A 2022 Commission preliminary review closed without a merits decision; AOM’s behaviour has increased since. 1.

Will the Commission assess AOM under Articles 101 and 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, including the mandatory free licence, members’ coordinated imposition of AOM technologies on third parties, and efforts to tip the market to AOM technologies?
Are gatekeepers’ mandates to use proprietary AOM formats with their platforms consistent with their interoperability and self-preferencing obligations under the DMA?

How does the Commission assess the long-term effects of the AOM model on European innovation and competition, and will it protect established standardisation processes (often created at European standards development organisations) from displacement by closed, proprietary consortia?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.9.2026) In 2022, the Commission opened a preliminary investigation into the Alliance for Open Media’s licensing policy for the AOMedia Video 1 (AV1) video codec. The investigation looked into its compliance with Article 101 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.

In 2023, the Commission closed its preliminary investigation on priority grounds, without any finding of either compliance or non-compliance of the conduct in question with EU competition rules. The Commission will continue to monitor the relevant market, notably for any competition concerns that AOM’s licensing policy may raise in the future.

The Digital Markets Act1 provides for clearly circumscribed obligations applicable to a set of pre-defined core platform services. The interoperability obligation applies to operating systems and virtual assistants, and the self-preferencing obligation applies to ranking in online social networks, online search engines, video sharing platforms, online intermediation services and virtual assistants.

The Commission will monitor the concerned gatekeepers’ conduct with a view to detecting and preventing any potential violation of a DMA obligation in relation to a designated core platform service. The ongoing reform of the EU Standardisation Regulation2 intends to make the European standardisation system future-proof and sustainable.

It responds to recent legal, market and geopolitical challenges, while preserving European values and regulatory autonomy. The Commission plans to adopt its proposal for a revised Regulation on 30 September 2026.
